opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. With text models, you have a lot of tasks where there's something close to a right answer. You can ask a math question, a coding problem, a factual question, and check whether the model got it. Even for open-ended writing, you can at least read the output and reason about it pretty directly, and language models themselves have gotten good enough to act as judges for a lot of those cases.

With images, almost everything is open-ended. If I ask for "a cozy cabin in the woods at dusk," there are infinitely many good answers, and no single reference image you can compare against. So the classic automated metrics, things like FID or CLIP score, end up measuring pretty coarse things. FID tells you whether your distribution of images looks statistically similar to some reference set, but it doesn't tell you whether a particular image is beautiful, or whether it actually followed the prompt, and it can be gamed or saturate in ways that don't track what people care about. CLIP score gives you rough text-image alignment, but it's notoriously bad at things like counting, spatial relationships, attribute binding, text rendering, all the details where models actually fail.

Then there's the fact that what makes an image good is so multidimensional. You have prompt adherence, aesthetics, photorealism or stylistic consistency, anatomical correctness, the absence of artifacts, diversity across samples, and these often trade off against each other. A model can get more aesthetically pleasing by collapsing toward a particular "look," and you lose diversity and controllability. Capturing that in one number is basically impossible.

Human evaluation is the gold standard, but it's expensive, slow, and noisy. Aesthetic preference varies a lot between people, and raters get fatigued or anchored on surface-level things like saturation and contrast rather than subtler correctness issues. Small differences, like a hand with six fingers in the corner, are easy to miss in a side-by-side comparison but matter a lot to real users.

And finally, as models get better, the evaluation problem gets harder, not easier. Early on, the failures were obvious. Now the top models are all quite good, so distinguishing them means looking at long-tail capabilities, specific use cases, and fine detail, which is exactly where our metrics are weakest. So a lot of the work has been building more targeted benchmarks, using vision-language models as judges with careful prompting and decomposition, and pairing that with well-designed human studies. But I'd say it's still very much an open problem.

r001.rationale: The response says image prompts can have “infinitely many good answers” and no single reference image, so there often is no clear right answer to evaluate against.

r002.rationale: It notes that aesthetic preferences vary between people, but does not state that a model change can improve perceived quality for one person while worsening it for another.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that with text, you often have something you can compare against. If you ask a model a question, there's usually a right answer, or at least a reference you can check against, and even for open-ended writing you can have people read it and judge whether it's correct, whether it's coherent. With images, the space of valid outputs is just enormous. If I say "a dog on a beach," there are essentially infinite images that satisfy that, and they can all be perfectly good while looking nothing like each other. So there's no ground truth to compare against.

And then the things we actually care about are things like, does it look real, does it match the prompt, is it aesthetically pleasing, does it have the right style. Those are really hard to pin down with a metric. People have used things like FID, which compares distributions of features, but that doesn't tell you much about any individual image, and it's surprisingly easy to get a good FID score with images that humans don't like, or vice versa. CLIP score helps with prompt alignment, but it also saturates and it misses a lot of fine-grained details, like counting objects or spatial relationships or text in the image.

So you end up falling back on human evaluation, which is expensive, it's slow, and it's noisy, because people genuinely disagree about what's a better image. One person cares about realism, another cares about composition, another about whether the hands look right. And that preference also shifts over time as people get used to what models can do. So you're trying to measure something that's subjective, multidimensional, and moving, with tools that mostly weren't designed for it. That's really the heart of why I think it's harder.

r001.rationale: The response says images have no ground truth to compare against and gives the example of many different images all satisfying the same prompt.

r002.rationale: The response notes that people value different image qualities and disagree about which image is better, but it does not explain that a model change could improve perceived quality for one person while worsening it for another.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that there isn’t a single correct answer. If I give you a prompt, there could be many very different images that all satisfy it. And then you have several dimensions you care about: Does the image look good? Does it actually follow the prompt? Is it coherent? Is it interesting? Those things don’t necessarily move together. You can have a beautiful image that completely ignores an important part of what you asked for.

Text has some of those same challenges, but in certain settings you have a more concrete way to check it. With code, for example, you can run it and see whether it passes tests. With images, a lot of the judgment is perceptual, and some of it is subjective. People can disagree about which image is better without either person being wrong.

So the challenge is finding an evaluation that captures what people actually value. An automated metric might capture one aspect of quality, but miss something that’s immediately obvious to a human. And human evaluations are expensive, plus you have to be very careful about what question you’re asking people to answer.

r001.rationale: It says many different images can satisfy a prompt and that people may disagree about which image is better without either being wrong.

r002.rationale: It notes that people can disagree about image quality, but does not state that changing a model can improve perceived quality for one person while worsening it for another due to differing preferences.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that there isn’t a single correct answer. For a given prompt, there can be many very different images that are all valid. And you’re evaluating several things at once: Does the image look good? Does it actually follow the prompt? Are the objects and their relationships correct? An image can be beautiful and still miss something fundamental that you asked for.

Text has some of that ambiguity too, but you can often evaluate it against a concrete outcome—whether an answer is correct or whether a piece of code passes a test. With images, even defining what success means can be more subjective. People might agree that one image looks more realistic, but disagree about which one better captures the intent of the prompt.

So the challenge is building an evaluation that captures those different dimensions without collapsing everything into a single score that hides the failures you actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response says there isn’t a single correct answer and that many different images can validly fit a prompt.

r002.rationale: It notes that people may disagree about which image better captures a prompt, but does not describe a model change improving quality for one person while worsening it for another.
